        The data show that there is a huge gap between Irrigation Potential Created (IPC)
and Irrigation Potential Utilized (IPU). The reasons behind such a situation are:
General wear and tear of the Irrigation Schemes together with non- availability of regular
fund for M&R works leading to loss of created potential.
Natural calamities like flood, storm etc. which cause damage to infrastructure of irrigation
schemes leading to loss of created potential.
        Erratic power supply in respect of the electrically operated irrigation schemes
(Surface Lift and Ground Water Lift) in some areas.
        Occasional damage of transformer, HT line and mechanical components at peak
hours of water requirement.
        Change of river course with respect to Surface Flow and Surface Lift irrigation
schemes.
        Livelihood shift by cultivators in the command areas of many schemes leading to
reduction in demand for irrigation water.
        Adherence of the cultivators in many areas to the traditional system of single
cropping and reluctance to adopt multiple cropping.
        Theft of motors/ pumps and other accessories in certain areas leading to non-
functioning of the irrigation schemes.
        For better utilization of Irrigation potential, 2352 Water Users’ Associations (WUA)
have been formed within the command areas of Irrigation schemes.

CHAPTER –VII


            FLOOD AND FLOOD CONRTROL MEASURES

                                                                                                  4




W       ater resources are essential for sustaining life, ecosystems, and human activities.
        They include surface water, such as rivers, lakes, and reservoirs, as well as
        groundwater stored in aquifers beneath the Earth's surface. These resources are
crucial for drinking, agriculture, industry, and energy production. However, their
availability is influenced by factors like climate change, population growth, and pollution,
leading to challenges in managing and conserving them sustainably. Efficient use,
pollution prevention, and integrated management practices are vital to ensuring that
water resources meet the needs of present and future generations.


    The State of Assam consists of two major valleys: the Brahmaputra Valley and the
Barak Valley. It is geographically located between 90° to 96° North Latitude and 24° to
28° East Longitude. Assam spans a total area of 78,438 square kilometers, with 56,194
square kilometers falling under the Brahmaputra Valley and 22,244 square kilometers,
including three hill districts, under the Barak Valley.


     The Brahmaputra Valley has an average width of approximately 80 kilometers. Its
principal river, the Brahmaputra, is one of the largest rivers globally, ranking fifth in terms
of average discharge. Originating from the Kailash ranges of the Himalayas at an elevation
of 5,300 meters, the river flows through Tibet before entering India via Arunachal Pradesh.
It traverses Assam and Bangladesh before emptying into the Bay of Bengal.The catchment
area of Brahmaputra in Tibet is 2,93,000 Sq. Km; in India and Bhutan is 2,40,000 Sq. Km
and in Bangladesh is 47,000 Sq. Km. The Brahmaputra basin extends over an area of
5,80,000 Sq. Km up to its confluence in Bangladesh.




                                                                                         93
                               Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




    The average width of Brahmaputra is 5.46 Km. the maximum discharge of
Brahmaputra at Pandu near Guwahati was recorded as 72,779 cumec on 23.08.62 and
minimum discharge was recorded as 1757 cumec on 22.02.63. The average annual
discharge is about 20,000 cumec and average dry season discharge is 4,420 cumec.
    The Barak valley has a geographical area of 6922.00 Sq. Km excluding 3(three) hill
districts. The local rainfall run off of the valley along with that of adjacent hilly areas flows
through river Barak and its various tributaries and is drained out to Bangladesh. The
Katakhal, Jiri, Chiri, Modhura, Longai, Sonai, Rukni and Singla are the main tributaries of
the valley. The tributaries are mainly rain fed and thus, cause flood problems when
precipitation occurs.
    Flood and erosion are two main natural disasters being faced by the state. The flood
prone area of the state is 31,500.00 Sq Km as assessed by the Rashtriya Barh Ayog. This
is about 39.58 % of the total land area of Assam and about 9.40% of total flood prone
area of the whole country. The flood prone area of the entire country stands at about 10.2
% of its total area. This shows that the flood prone area of Assam is four times the national
mark of the flood prone area of the country. Records show that average annual area
affected by flood is 9.31 Lakh Hectares. The flood protected area of the state is 16500.00
Sq. Km till date.
    The severity of the flood problem in the state has been further aggravated by acute
erosion on both banks of river Brahmaputra and its tributaries. Study reveals that an area
of 4.27 Lakh Hectare of the state has been eroded by the rivers since 1950, which is 7.40
% of area of the state. The average annual rate of erosion is 8000.00 Ha.
     Assam had three waves of flood in the year 2025, causing substantial loss of lives and
property and severely impacting the economy of the State. Out of total 35 districts of
Assam, 28 districts have been affected by flood in this year affecting approximately 11.19
lakh people in 3,255 villages. The death toll due to floods and landslides has been 36.
Besides, substantial damages to standing crops, infrastructures like, roads, bridges,
irrigation facilities, health facilities, schools, Livestock population etc. has also been
reported from the affected districts and respective line departments.
   As such, based on the damage reports received from the Districts and the
Departments, fund requirement is estimated to be Rs. 2871.21 crore which includes an
amount of Rs 62.98 Cr. for rescue and relief operation, Rs. 10.26 Cr. for sectoral damages
other than Core Critical Infrastructure (like Fish seeds, Replacement of Animals,
Assistance to Small and Marginal Farmers and Assistance to Artisans), Rs. 28.23 for
damages in Housing Sector and Rs. 2769.74 Cr. for repairing and restoration of immediate
nature for various infrastructure damaged during the flood.


POPULATION AFFECTED BY FLOOD
    Assam is one of the most flood prone states in India. The State faces acute flood
problem in the flood plains of the river Brahmaputra and Barak and other smaller river
sub-basins. The extremely dynamic monsoon regime vis-à-vis the unique physiographic
setting of the basin has been considered as the single most important cause for frequent
occurrence of flood in this region. Historical analysis of the last fifteen years shows the
problem of flood and its impact on the population every year.




   94
                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




                 Source: Assam Flood Memorendum 2025, ASDMA




FLOOD AND EROSION PROBLEM OF THE STATE
    The Brahmaputra and Barak rivers, along with their 48 major tributaries and countless
sub-tributaries, crisscross the plains of both valleys. Flooding, bank erosion, and drainage
congestion are significant challenges faced by the state during the monsoon season.
Flooding is a recurring phenomenon in this region, with multiple waves of floods causing
extensive damage each year. The losses incurred by people in terms of property, crops,
and livestock are enormous, amounting to hundreds of crores annually. Additionally,
severe damage is inflicted on roads, bridges, schools, communication systems, and other
infrastructure. These losses diminish the nation's wealth and adversely affect the state's
development. During the post-independence period, Assam has faced major floods in
1954, 1962, 1972, 1977, 1984, 1988, 1998, 2002, 2004, 2008, 2014, 2016 etc. Almost
every year, three to four waves of flood ravage the flood prone areas of Assam. The
average annual loss due to flood in Assam is to the tune of Rs. 200.00 Crores.
   In 1954, the country witnessed unprecedented floods following which the Govt.
of India announced a National Policy on Floods comprising of three phases viz.-

     ➢ The immediate,
     ➢ The short term and
     ➢ The long term measures.

        As per the Flood Hazard Atlas of Assam prepared by National Remote Sensing
        Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad using satellite data, about 28.75% (22.54 lakh
        hectares) of land in Assam state is affected by flood during 1998-2015.

   The flood control activities in Assam started mainly after the announcement of National
Water Policy. Subsequently, “Outlined plan for flood control in Assam” along with various
comprehensive plans were prepared and the priority areas that require immediate and
urgent attention were identified.

Assam Floods in 2025:
    This year , Assam has faced three waves of floods till date, which have affected 28
districts of the state, resulting in loss of human lives, livestock and large scale damage to
the dwelling houses, standing crops, infrastructure like roads, bridges, embankments,
schools, AWCs etc.
    Notified Flood season starts in Assam from 1st May till 31st October every year and
during the period ASDMA generates daily flood situation reports digitally through DRIMS
(Disaster Reporting and Information Management System). Each Revenue Circle of Assam
submits an online situation report through its respective DDMAs in the DRIMS portal.
Following 28 districts of Assam have been affected by floods this year viz. Barpeta,
Biswanath, Bongaigaon, Cachar, Charaideo, Darrang, Dhemaji, Dibrugarh, Dima-Hasao,
Goalpara, Golaghat, Hailakandi, Hojai, Jorhat, Kamrup, Kamrup (M), Karbi Anglong,
Kokrajhar, Majuli, Morigaon, Nagaon, Sivasagar, Sonitpur, South Salmara, Sribhumi,
Tinsukia, Lakhimpur and West Karbi Anglong as per Assam state Disaster Mnagement
Authority Flood Memorandum Report 2025.




     98
                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



Flood Waves in Assam, 2025


    The 2025 flood season in Assam occurred in three distinct waves. The first wave (31
May–22 July) was the most severe, affecting 26 districts, 2,630 villages, and over 1.04
lakh people, with 24 human lives lost. The second wave (7 Aug–5 Sept) was milder in
spread, impacting 11 districts and 412 villages, with lower population impact (45,930)
and one death in urban flood. The third wave (12 Sept–13 Oct) again affected 11 districts
and 468 villages, with population affected rising to 1.08 lakh, and 2 human lives lost.
Overall, the data indicates that the first wave was the most destructive, while later waves
caused localized but significant impacts.

Assam Integrated River Basin Management Programme (AIRBMP)


   Assam is among the states hardest hit by erosion flood hazards. Climate change is
expected to exacerbate current hazards and lead to more frequent floods and accelerated
soil erosion. Therefore, a progressive and systematic approach is needed to address the
key water-related risks and opportunities in Assam. A critical first step is the development
of an enabling institutional framework and building the capacities of relevant agencies for
IWRM and DRM. These include the Assam Water Resources Department (WRD), Assam


                                                                                      99
                               Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA), and Flood and River Erosion Management
Agency of Assam (FREMAA). Also, an IWRM approach integrates green infrastructure with
grey infrastructure, such as flood embankments, river erosion works, and dams offers the
best approach for cost-effective and resilient infrastructure. Non-structural solutions such
as flood forecasting and early warning, emergency preparation, disaster response, and
recovery are also necessary to fully address all elements of the DRM cycle of mitigation,
preparedness, response, and recovery. Stakeholders include diverse river constituencies
and users with varying levels of representation in local govt. bodies, incentives, and
power.


   The Government of Assam, through Govt. of India, approached the World Bank to
provide support to its agenda for strengthening IWRM and DRM through the ongoing
Assam Integrated River Basin Management Program (AIRBMP). The Program               focuses
on strengthening institutions, filling critical knowledge gaps, and implementing integrated
solutions through a structured basin-wise planning process to tackle the current
challenges of floods and erosion, amongst others, and to seize opportunities for climate-
resilient growth and improved livelihood. The Department has taken up AIRBMP with a
loan of $500 million and counterpart funding of $125 Million from the World Bank. Under
Phase (I) of this program, two River Basins, one at Buridehing River and the other at Beki
River, have been selected for undertaking river works under no-regret investment. The
river works are as follows:-

Climate Resilient Brahmaputra Integrated Flood and River Erosion River
Management Programme (CRBIFRERMP)
    The Project will focus on the main stem of the Brahmaputra River and apply a holistic,
integrated, and risk-informed approach to manage river bank erosion and the attendant
flood risk. The institutional capacity of Assam and the affected communities will be
strengthened to enhance the climate and disaster reliance of the investment. By stabilizing
60 km of river banks, placing 32 km of pro-siltation measures, and constructing or
rehabilitating 4 km of climate resilient embankments in five high-priority districts, the
project will: (i) secure living spaces, (ii) reduce erosion and flooding, (iii) support-
livelihoods and small farmers, (iv) create employment of opportunities for the most
vulnerable riverine poor, and (v) ultimately enhance the navigability of the river.


    To increase the long-term reliability and effectiveness of planning and implementing
flood and river bank erosion risk management in Assam, the project will advance key
WRD knowledge of modern survey practices, flood forecasting and early warning systems,
erosion prediction, embankment breach models, management, asset management, risk-
sensitive land use planning, and pilot nature-based solutions. The project seeks to
optimize co-benefits, promote data sharing, and empower women through economic
activities, enabling them to better respond to climate changes and disasters. The project
is expected to benefit about 10 lakh people. The Department has taken up ADB New Loan
of $200 Million and counterpart funding of $55 Million for the first phase. The projects are
targeted for flood and erosion management in the main stream Brahmaputra and have
been proposed in (i) Dibrugarh - Tinsukia, (ii) Morigaon, (iii) Kamrup Rural, and (v)
Goalpara. The scope of the project will include bio-engineering activities using nature-
based solutions for embankment slope stabilization and bank protection work.


Preparedness measures taken by ASDMA before floods:
    As part of the flood preparedness initiatives, Assam State Disaster Management
Authority (ASDMA) had conducted six thematic meetings for flood preparedness during
March- April 2025 with all line departments, Central Agencies and stakeholders. These
thematic meetings are viz. (i) Coordination for Response with responding agencies, (ii)
Critical Infrastructure Preparedness, (iii) Ensuring continuity of services viz. Health, Water
& Sanitation, Education, Social welfare services etc., (iv) Relief Camp Management, (v)
Risk communication and (vi) Reporting and Damage Assessment as part of its
preparedness this year with various stakeholders.


    Besides, ASDMA also conducted multi layered review of Flood Preparedness, which
includes- (i) Flood Preparedness Review Meeting by His Excellency Governor of Assam on
28th May, 2025, (ii) Video Conference with the District Commissioners by Hon’ble Chief
Minister on 30th May 2025, (iii) District level Flood Preparedness review by Hon’ble
Minister, Revenue & DM Department, Assam along with field visit in 6 districts (24th –
26th May, 2025), (iv) State Level Flood Preparedness Review Meeting by Hon’ble Chief
Secretary, Assam on 17th May, 2025, (v) Video conferencing with the DDMAs to review
flood preparedness at the district level conducted on 27th March 2025.



                                                                                       101
                             Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




    NDRF teams from 1st Bn. and 12th Bn. have been pre-positioned at eight (8) strategic
locations of the state of Assam namely Silchar, Jorhat, Barpeta, Bongaigaon (1st Bn.
NDRF), Dibrugarh, Tezpur, Sivasagar and Titabor (12th Bn. NDRF) for effective and
prompt response during flood. Besides, five companies of State Disaster Response Force
(SDRF) were also deployed in 58 locations of Assam along with rescue boats and deep
divers. Besides, ASDMA also deployed rescue boats, AAPDA Mitra volunteers and DDRF
teams in selected locations in certain vulnerable locations. These proactive preparedness
measures lead to substantive reduction of human lives lost and properties during the flood
as compared to the severity of the flood situation.


    Further, ASDMA receives FLEWS (Flood Early Warning System) alerts from North
Eastern Space Application Centre (NESAC) within 12 to 48 hrs lead time in the category
of Low, Moderate, High and Very High alerts and these alerts are disseminated to DDMAs,
Revenue Circle Offices, concerned authorities of the Govt. of Assam and other response
agencies.


Conclusion:


    Hon’ble Chief Minister of Assam reviewed the flood preparedness of the state on 30th
May, 2025 involving District Commissioners of all DDMAs of Assam. Hon’ble Chief Minister
instructed all the District Commissioners to establish effective coordination with NDRF and
SDRF teams, to ensure a prompt response when required. Further, His Excellency
Governor of Assam on 28th May, 2025 also took stock of the Flood preparedness for state
of Assam.


    Based on the ground assessment by the District Administrations, District Disaster
Management Authorities (DDMAs) and concerned line departments of the State
Government, total requirement of funds covered under SDRF/NDRF for (i) rescue & relief
operation (₹62.98 crores), (ii) Sectoral damages other than core Critical Infrastructure
(Fish seeds, Replacement of Animals, Assistance to Small and Marginal Farmers,
Assistance to Artisans) (₹10.26 crores), (iii) Damages in Housing Sector (₹28.23 crores)
and (iv) Damages in Core Critical Infrastructure (₹2769.74 crores). Therefore total
estimated fund requirement for various work is amounting to ₹ 2871.21 Cr. (in words Two
Thousand Eight hundred Seventy One Crore and Twenty one Lakhs only)


   Government of India is therefore, requested to provide financial assistance and help
the State to recover from the severe damages caused by the multiple waves of floods in
2025

 CHAPTER – VIII

 LIVESTOCK, ANIAML HUSBANDRY & DIARY DEVELOPMENT




    A     nimal Husbandry is potentially one of the most important sectors for the rapid
          socio-economic development of the state. Assam's economy is predominately
          agrarian, with more than 70% of the population. The animal husbandry sector
significantly impacts employment generation in the state and plays a vital role in income
generation in both rural and semi-urban economies. The Animal Husbandry and
Veterinary Department of the State has been implementing various socio-economic
programmes to create gainful employment opportunities in rural areas through various
developmental schemes to boost the socio-economic condition of the rural economy and
act to enhance the volume of livestock and poultry products in the State to reduce the
gap between demand and supply of these products.
     For many poor families in rural areas, livestock can be a valuable asset and source
of income, especially as climate change and limited land squeeze traditional farming in
the state. They also enable diversification of land use and ensure the nutritional security
of the population. The State government is investing in veterinary services, vaccinations,
and increasing technology accessibility to reduce livestock mortality in the state. The
main objective of the Department of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary in the state is
twofold such as to provide health coverage to the livestock and poultry and to undertake
livestock developmental activities for improving state income and raising the standard of
living of the people. Various initiatives such as breed improvement programs, artificial
insemination, and disease control measures have already been undertaken while Mobile
Veterinary Unit (MVU) is introduced to provide door-to-door animal health services.


                                                                                     103
                             Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




Efforts are being made to protect animal health and minimize infection risks, as well as
disease control and monitoring to augment the production of annual products.

    To achieve this goal, the Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Department of the State
has been providing animal health care services and breed improvement facilities through
21 veterinary hospitals, 297 dispensaries, 767 Sub-Centre/First Aid Centre/SMC, 134
Block Veterinary Dispensaries, 8 Key Village Centre etc. However, the existence of a large
and low productive population of non-descript animals and birds, the State has to depend
on the import of livestock products from outside the State to meet the increasing demand.

LIVESTOCK POPULATION AS PER 20TH LIVESTOCK CENSUS
    According to the 20th Livestock Census 2019, the Cattle population constitutes the the
largest group with more then ten million. Out of the total Cattle indigenous/non-descript
cattle comprises 1.1 crore while crossbreed cattle population comprises 7.7 lakhs. Buffalo
comprises 4.2 lakhs while Sheep was counted to become 3.3 lakhs numbers. Goat and Pig
comprised of about 43.15 lakh and 21 lakhs numbers respectively during Livestock Census
2019.

ASSAM PROJECT ON AGRI-BUSINESS AND RURAL TRANSFORMATION (APART)


    After the successful completion of the Assam Rural Infrastructure and Agriculture
Service (ARIASP) and Assam Agricultural Competitiveness Project (AACP), the
Government of Assam through the Government of India has received a loan from the
World Bank for the implementation of Assam Agri-business and Rural Transformation
Project (APART).


Project Development Objective (PDO): “To add value and improve the resilience of
selected agriculture value chains, focusing on smallholder farmers and agro-
entrepreneurs in targeted districts of Assam”.


The project broadly focuses on two components under APART:


1. PORK VALUE CHAIN (PVC): To be implemented by the Animal Husbandry & Veterinary
    Department (AHVD).

2. MILK VALUE CHAIN (MVC)
    a. Formal Milk Value Chain: Being implemented by West Assam Milk Producers’
       Cooperative Union Limited (WAMUL).

    b. Informal Milk Value Chain: Being implemented by the Dairy Sector by the Dairy
       Development Department (DDD).

     1. APART Strategy- Pig Sector Intervention

           Knowledge, attitude & practice gap analysis of all the value chain actors,
            customized designing of training content for capacity building and
            massive awareness programme on good production practices & food




  108
                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



              safety along the value chain.

            Formation of Farmer Producer Organization (FPO) in production clusters
             to undertake the various activities in a group basis and organized way
             which is difficult to perform by an individual farmer


     2. MILK VALUE CHAIN (MVC): APART Strategy
        Dairy Sector Intervention: FORMAL SECTOR

             The focus is productivity enhancement by organizing farmers into Milk
            Producers’ Institutions (MPIs) that eventually will get registered as Dairy
            Cooperative Societies (DCS) and genetic upgradation of non-descript cows
            using AI, improved feeding through fodder production demonstrations, bulk
            supplements provision through DCS and by developing linkages with crop
            producers (e.g. maize, mustard, legumes for crop residue).


Piggery Development
Pig Development Schemes undertaken by the A. H. & Veterinary Department,
Assam:


    Assam is characterized by a high proportion of tribal people for whom pig-keeping is
integral in their way of life. The present population scenario of pigs in Assam comprises
non-descript local varieties, exotic hybrids and genetically graded pigs. However, the
large majority of the pig population in this part of the country belongs to the non-descript
type. The schemes in operation under pig development are as follows:
               National Livestock Mission (NLM)
               Rastriya Krishi Vikash Yojana (RKVY)
               Assam Agri-Business and Rural Transformation Project (APART)
               Assam Milk, Meat and Egg Mission Society (AMMEMS) under CMSGUY.
               Different pig development schemes under SOPD-G, TSP, SCCP etc.


Govt. Pig Farms:


    There are 19 Nos. of Govt. Pig Farms in the state. Out of 19 Nos. of Govt. Pig Farms,
10 Nos. are functional, but with lower capacity. The department is taking every possible
step to make all the farms functional to their full strength with funds from different
schemes like SOPDG, RIDF etc.


POULTRY DEVELOPMENT:
   The Animal Husbandry & Veterinary Department, Assam is encouraging backyard
poultry rearing in the state for enhancing meat ad egg production. As this sector generates
employment and enhance rural income, a large number of people are directly engaged in
poultry sector in the state

DETAILED ACTIVITIES RELEVANT TO DISEASE PREVENTION THROUGH
INSTITUTE OF VETERINARY BIOLOGICALS, FOR THE YEAR 2021-22, 2022-23,
2023-2024

   Agriculture still remains the backbone of the Indian economy and it provides employment
to majority of the population. Agriculture plays a vital role not only in providing food
and nutrition to the people, but also in the supply of raw material to industries and to
export trade. It is understood that without a sustainable and productive growth of the
agricultural sector, the other types of development in any sphere will be unstable and illusory.
The increase in growth of human population has undoubtedly excreted pressure on agriculture
and livestock. Even than the annual growth rate of cattle and buffalo continued to sustain
mainly because of economic compulsion and increase realization on the part of the farmer
about the value of the animals and also due to the fact that various dreaded disease of
livestock could be effectively controlled by the effort of the veterinarian.



DISEASE STATUS IN THE STATE OF ASSAM

   At present, HS and FMD are the two most pre-dominating large animal diseases of
the state in relation to the economy of the people. Out of four FMD serotypes prevailing in this
state, the maximum number of outbreaks is found to be due to Type- ‘O’. Among the
economically important diseases, Haemorrhagic Septicemia is considered to be one of the
major diseases occurring mostly in the riverine areas of the state and causing substantial
economic losses to the farmers in general. The disease occurs just at the beginning of the
monsoon and during and after the flood. It occurs throughout the state but are more prevalent
in the 23 flood affected districts out of 33 districts of the state and simultaneously the diseases
like B.Q and Anthrax are also appearing sporadically parallel to HS posing severe threat to the
bovine population. Other major diseases that occur in Assam are Ranikhet disease, duck
plague, duck cholera, pigeon pox, enterotoxaemia, sheep and goat pox, fowl plague etc
and many parasitic infestations.



IMMUNIZATIONPROGRAMME

   Immunization Programme in Assam has been taken up through Central Sector Schemes
like ASCAD, CFS-CP, PPR-EP, and NADCP and also through different veterinary dispensary and
sub-center of the state by procuring vaccine produced at Biological Production Unit of
Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Department located at Khanapara Guwahati-22.

CATTLE BREEDING PROJECT (CCBP)

Our Non-Descriptive Indigenous Cattle & Buffaloes are the main source of milk production
with their very low production potentiality. So, their genetic improvement has become
the top priority. CCBP, (S.E) Phase- I was launched under NPCBB with the objective to
produce Milch Cattle economically in large numbers for enhancement of milk production
to be achieved through infusion of exotic inheritance, and also to combine productivity
and adaptability to disease resistance including reasonable draught ability to meet the
local requirements.

Physical and financial achievements of NERDDL & Animal Health Centre

(2024-2025 and 2025-2026)



           The North Eastern Regional Disease Diagnostic Laboratory (NERDDL) established in
Guwahati in 2023 with 100% assistance from Government of India as the Referral
Laboratory for the North East States. It provided referral and consultancy services to the
state diagnostic laboratories of the region for                                                                                       economically important livestock and
poultry diseases, as and when needed. It is the only laboratory to diagnose exotic
diseases like African Swine Fever (ASF), Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD), Avian Influenza,
Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) for NE States. It is also working with 2 (Two)
collaborative project on “Diagnosis and control of zoonotic diseases” with integrated
Diseases Surveillance Program (IDSP) of Rural Health Mission and Collaborative project
under DBT on “Establishment of a Consortium for One Health to Address Zoonotic and
Trans boundary Disease in India including the North East Region” with Department of Bio-
technology, Government of India.

Schemes implemented by Directorate of Dairy Development, Assam under
State Owned Priority Development (SOPD)

Enhancement of Overall Milk Production in Assam
     The farmers are the backbone of the dairy industry in Assam. Typically, the farmers
      of Assam are marginal dairy farmers producing on an average 2 lts of milk per day
      and they are geographically dispersed. Hence there is need to help build robust and
      strong farmer’s organization like Dairy Cooperative Societies. Seed money to 144
      Nos of Dairy Cooperative Societies has been provided in the financial year 2022-
      23 in order to achieve this. This has benefit about 4000 marginal dairy farmers of the
      state directly.
     In order to enhance profitability and competitiveness of our dairy farmers the
      directorate of dairy development has helped in the formation of Dairy Co-operative
      Societies (DCS) and provided input support and training to the members of the DCS
      under the scheme “Integrated Support Services for creation of milk surplus districts
      at Sadiya subdivision”
     In order to facilitate dairy business in the state of Assam, the scheme Establishment
      of Commercial Dairy Units is being implemented by the department which will
      support 17 nos of progressive dairy entrepreneurs. This is expected to enhance the
      milk production in the state and promote scientific dairy farming
     In the financial year 2022-23, 1.16 lakh doses of Sex Sorted Semen was procured
      by the Dairy Development, Assam which will result in production of about 50
      thousand female calves. In the financial year 2023-24 also, 1.00 Lakh sex sorted
      semen for an amount of Rs. 810 lakh was procured. This initiative is undertaken to
      increase the female population of high yielding breeds and productive cattle which is
      expected to increase the milk production in the state.
     Processing capacity was established by the Dairy Development Department, Assam
      and is to be operationalized in collaboration with WAMUL (West Assam Milk Producers
      Union Limited).

Scheme wise targets and achievements under World Bank Aided Project
(APART) for the last three years.

     Dairy in the state is characterized by rural smallholder and subsistence production
systems along with specialized dairy production belts (with improved cattle) in urban and
peri-urban areas. The traditional market (informal) with either fresh liquid milk or milk
products accounts for about 95% of the market opportunities for farmers. It is thus
apparent that the development of the traditional market will be extremely important for
the Assam dairy sub-sector as it transits to a more formal way of operating, and therefore
it is necessary to inject interventions that could facilitate improvement of the market. The
major objective of the Dairy Development Department under the Assam Agribusiness and
Rural Transformation Project (APART) is the transformation of the informal Dairy Value
Chain into a formal one through improved resilience in Production, Quality, Safety and
Standards of Milk by adding value to the product with particular focus on informal market
actors and dairy entrepreneurs in targeted project districts.


   The project districts covered under APART - Dairy Development are Nagaon, Sonitpur,
Barpeta, Karbi Anglong, Kamrup, Dhubri, Golaghat, Kokrajhar, Lakhimpur, Darrang,
Cachar, Hailakandi, Sivasagar, Jorhat, Goalpara, Morigaon, Nalbari, Bongaigaon and
Bajali.
To achieve the project objective, the Directorate of Dairy Development has taken up the
following activities with support from knowledge partner, International Livestock
Research Institute (ILRI), Kenya:
1. Market assessment through mapping of market actors of informal Dairy Value Chain
   through Physical assessment of the distribution of market actors in 19 project
   districts.
2. Assessment of human health risk in Dairy Value Chain with particular focus on the
   informal sector before and after interventions by assessment of the magnitude of risk
   from Milk and Milk Products, assessment of adulteration, microbial load, antimicrobial
   residue and aflatoxin, assessment of the prevalence of zoonotic pathogens like
   Brucella, Mycobacterium etc. and identification of critical control points.
3. Improvement and strengthening of the Lab infrastructure in dairy plants for checking
   quality and safety of milk /milk products traded by informal market actors.
   Improvement in quality in the traditional market will raise the demand and value of
   the products and thus income and employment. It will also help facilitate the evolution
   of the traditional market towards the more regulated and organized market.
4. Design, Development and Printing of training manuals for Informal Milk Market Actors,
   protocols for Training of Trainers (ToT), capacity building of Govt. Officials on
   Laboratory Technology with support from International Livestock Research Institute
   (ILRI).
5. Training of milk market actors – Training of milk market actors in targeted project
   districts on improved package of practices for quality and hygiene. The milk market
   actors comprise Milk Producers, Milk Traders, Sweet Makers, and Cottage Processors.
6. Formation of DCS among the interested trained Milk Producers - The transformation
   is sought to achieve through mobilizing the informal Dairy value chain through the
   strengthening of the existing Dairy Cooperatives Societies, the formation of new Dairy
   Cooperatives Societies wherever feasible and register them under the Assam
   Cooperatives Registration Act. They will be supported with capacity up-gradation,
   input services, market access and other linkages in the Milk value chain.

                                                                                      119
                                 Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




7. Linkages and Support to Market actors to run their business efficiently by providing
   input support and recognition for adoption of improved practices.
8. Assessment of critical need gap of existing DCS and arrangement for need-based
   support. Need-based interventions/ support will be provided for capacity building,
   value addition and technical up gradation.
9. Demonstration of Mastitis and Reproductive Health Management camp on a pilot basis
   to create awareness among the dairy farmers regarding diagnosis and management
   of mastitis and reproductive diseases in targeted clusters.

 CHAPTER – IX


                                      FISHERIES


                                                                                                4




T
       he fishery sector in Assam occupies a significant place in the Socio-economics
       development in the State. It has been recognised as a vital sector for both income
       and employment generation. Assam is endowed with vast water resources in the
form of ponds, derelict water bodies and beels/floodplain wetlands etc. covering 2.59 lakh
hectares. Besides this the two major river systems i.e., the mighty Brahmaputra and the
Barak with its tributaries which spread up to 11304 Km as a riverine Fishery. Thus, the
entire water spread areas have immense opportunities to boost fish production and
promote ample employment opportunities as well as livelihood to the society and nutrition
to the individual health. There are also 216 freshwater fish species and over 50 species of
ornamental importance.
     Considering the socio-economic importance of the sector and the untapped natural
fishery resources of the State, both the Central and State Governments have given special
thrust to this sector to make the state self-sufficient in fish production as well as to make
the State, a hub of fish export to the neighbouring states and the countries. Accordingly,
the State Fisheries Department has been implementing several development schemes and
programmes for sustainable development of the sector playing an important role in solving
various issues of the fish farmer and fishery entrepreneur contributing technical
backstopping as well as facilitating financial and material help to them and thereby
creating ample scope of employment opportunities.

production potential to the optimum level in a sustainable manner.

   The major functions of the Department for the overall development of the fishery sector
are:

    To increase fish and quality fish seed production in the state with optimum utilization
     of resources


    Implementation of Fishery related schemes of the Government of Assam and
     Government of India,


    To identify and promote research and studies on fisheries and fishery-related areas
     so that benefits can be disseminated to the grass-level users,


    To collect, compile, analyze and make available adequate/relevant statistical and
     other information for proper planning to promote fish farming and related
     industries/activities,


    To prepare/support in preparation/project reports and proposals related to Fisheries
     and fishery-related industries,

    To provide extension services to Fish farmers/fishermen and fishery entrepreneurs.

PRESENT STATUS OF DEVELOPMENT AND MANAGEMENT OF RESOURCES

     Fish production in the state has reached a level of 5.29 lakh MT during the year 2024-
25 against the estimated nutritional demand of 5.25 lakh MT considering per capita
consumption of 15.22 Kg/yr. The Department has taken some fish production enhancing
strategies such as horizontal expansion of the fish culture area through the creation of
New Pond construction, New Rearing Tank construction, Reclamation and Renovation of
existing areas for pisciculture and converting low lying area to Community Tank. Further,
emphasis has been given to the adoption of advanced technologies such as Recirculatory
Aquaculture System (RAS), Biofloc, and Recreational Fishery etc. along with diversification
of cultural techniques.


       River ranching programme, and fingerling stocking at wetlands are also introduced as
special activities under Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) for augmenting
and enhancing the natural productivity of river and beel through the release of quality fish
seed. Simultaneously, the pen and cage culture activities are implemented under the
CMSGUY scheme in some beel and wetland.


       The revenue fisheries, i.e. rivers and beels are at present under the control of Assam
Fisheries      Development      Corporation   Ltd;   Fisheries   Administrative   Departments,
Government of Assam; Deputy Commissioners and Sub-Divisional Officers (Civil) and
Panchayats through leasing out to individual /Co-operative societies. Moreover, few farms
and low-lying areas are managed by FISHFED by itself or through leasing.

Brief descriptions of the schemes/programmes implemented by the Fishery
Department in the last three years are:

A. State Owned Priority development (SOPD) schemes

 1. Fish & Fish Seed Farming
      This is one of the major schemes implemented by the Department for the
      enhancement of fish and fish seed production along with other related activities and
      infrastructure development. Various programmes have been taken up under this
      scheme for the enhancement of fish and fish seed production. The following major
      beneficiary-oriented activities have been implemented under this scheme including
      general area and SCSP:
        a) Extension of fish culture area
        b) Upgradation and renovation of the Departmental Farm
        c) Input and material Supply for increasing Fish productivity in Beneficiaries Pond
           as well as in departmental Farms




  130
                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



        d) Development of water bodies through co-operative society under SCSP and
           supply of fish culture input in existing ponds under TSP
    Additionally, a five-year project titled “Gene Bank - Scientific Conservation Programme
for Indigenous Fish (SCoPIF)” is being implemented covering both experimental and
natural habitats by involving the College of Fisheries, Raha. The project aims at conserving
the fish biodiversity of the State with a scientific approach for the development of
standardized propagation technology for selected endangered fish species to suit the local
environment, developing a directory of indigenous fish species along with a database and
establishing a fish gene bank.
2.   Fishery Extention Service
     Activities like the engagement of Matsya Mitra (Contractual Fishery extension worker);
     observation of National/International Fish related festivals etc., advertisement,
     publicity, Organisation/participation in the exhibition including publication of the
     Annual Administrative Report etc. are mainly implemented through this scheme.
3.   Marketing and Transport of fish
     Marketing of fish in hygienic conditions is one of the important aspects for consumer
     safety as well as encouraging more and more people to take up fisheries as a
     livelihood. The development of fish marketing infrastructure in the form of hygienic
     fish markets and retail outlets has been taken up under this scheme.


B. Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF): Department of Fisheries, Assam
   has been implementing different fishery-related infrastructure development
   programmes under NABARD instituted Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF),
   contributing towards agricultural growth, rural connectivity and other social sector
   development. Under RIDF-XXVI, 3 major projects have been implemented and under
   different stages of achievement. The schemes are (I) 4-wheeler refrigerated Fish
   Carrying Vehicles with a physical target of 70 vehicles (II) the Establishment of 44 Mini
   Fish Feed Plant and 5 Medium Fish Feed Plant and (III) 3- Wheeler fish carrying vehicles
   with insulated Ice Boxes.
     In addition, the NABARD has accorded sanction for the development of 23
     departmental existing fish farms under RIDF-XXVIII with an approved fund provision
     of Rs. 6413.96 lakh. The scheme will be implemented shortly.


C. CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES

 I. Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY): The PMMSY is an umbrella
   scheme with two separate components namely (a) Central Sector Scheme and (b)
   Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) component is further segregated into non-
   beneficiary oriented and beneficiary oriented scheme. Non-beneficiary-oriented
   component to be implemented by the State Government, the entire project cost will
   be shared between centre and state as 90% central share and 10% state share. In
   beneficiary-oriented components, the fund sharing pattern is 60:40 (Beneficiary share:
   Govt. share) for the general category and for SC/ST/Women category fund sharing
   pattern is 40:60 (Beneficiary share: Govt. share). The following are the main
   components implemented under PMMSY:

II.   NATIONAL WELFARE FUND FOR FISHERMEN

Group Accident Insurance Scheme (GAIS) Under PRADHAN MANTRI MATSYA
SAMPADA YOJANA (PMMSY)

    Group Accident Insurance Scheme (GAIS) is now a sub-component of Pradhan Mantri
Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY) from 2020-21 and its implementing authority is the
National Fisheries Development Board (NFDB) which was earlier implemented by
FISHCOPFED. Fishermen, fish workers, fish farmers and any other categories of persons
directly involved in fishing and fisheries-related allied activities collectively called “Fishers”
are covered under the Group Accident Insurance Scheme (GAIS). Men or women fishers
who are in the age group from 18 years to 70 years as identified by the State/UT fisheries
department are insured under the scheme in two Policies i.e. Group Janata Personal
Accident Insurance (GJPA) and Special Contingency Policy. Under GJPA the fishers shall
be eligible for insurance coverage up to Rs.5.00 lakh for “Death” or “Permanent total
disability”. Under the Special Contingency Policy, it is up to Rs. 2.50 lakh for “Permanent
partial disability” and Rs. 25,000 for “Accidental hospitalization”. The premium for both
policies is free for the insurers. The premium will be borne by and shared between the
Central and State Governments in the ratio of 90:10 for North Eastern and Himalayan
States. The Insurance cover will be for a period of 12 months and the premium shall be
paid annually.


D. FISHERY MISSION SOCIETY UNDER CMSGUY

    The Fishery Mission Society for Chief Ministers Samagra Grammya Unnayan Yojana
(FMS-CMSGUY) is an autonomous Society under the administrative control of Mega Mission
Society for Chief Minister Samagra Gramya Unnayan Yojana (MMS-CMSGUY) and Fisheries
Department, Government of Assam. It is formed to contribute to achieving the goal of
doubling the farm income of fish farmers in Assam in terms of fish and fish seed production
by developing existing water resources through effective resource utilization scientifically
and the creation of additional water bodies for large-scale fish production in a scientific
way. The Fishery Mission Society also aims at Quality fish seed production and distribution
at the farmer’s doorstep and conservation of native, endangered and indigenous fish
species by diffusing useful knowledge and extending doorstep technical support.

E. ASSAM AGRIBUSINESS AND RURAL TRANSFORMATION PROJECT (APART)

Sub-Component: Fisheries Value Chain

The fish value chain is to be implemented by the Department of Fisheries and the district
ATMA, in collaboration with the World Fish Centre (WFC) and private sector partners. This
sub-component will focus on: (i) improving the quality of the inputs such as fish seed and
feed for aquaculture, (ii) increasing the fish productivity and production from the
pond/tank aquaculture systems, (iii) increasing fish production through culture-cum-
capture fisheries activities in the beels, (iv) promoting diversification of fish species –
particularly genetically improved strains - in combination with Indian major carps in the
culture systems, (v) improved post-harvest management, value addition and marketing
of produce by setting up fish farmer common service centres (CSCs.).
F. Kisan Credit Card (KCC) to Fish Farmers: The Union Government, in the budget
2018-19 announced their decision to extend the facility of KCC to the farmers of Animal
Husbandry and Fisheries to help them acquire loan from commercial banks, RRBs, Small
Finance Banks and Cooperatives for readily purchasing pisciculture inputs such as fish
seed, fish feed, lime, medicines, net, boat, vessels, bicycle/tricycle with vessels for fish
harvest and for fish marketing purposes. The District-level machinery of the Fishery
Department facilitates and guides the fish farmers, fishers and fish traders to obtain KCC
and to submit applications to the banks in a holistic approach.

CHAPTER-X

                                      FORESTRY




A
      ssam is a rainbow state with blue rivers and green hills, a unique bio-diversity
      treasure house of rare flora, fauna, and forests. This land is described as "Mung-
      Dun- Chun- Kham" or the "Country of Golden Land” by the Ahom Rulers. Forest and
trees are the very basis of life on our planet. Forestry is a vital sector of the State. The
United Nations Forum on Forests 15 recognizes that over 1.6 billion people depend on
forest for subsistence, livelihood, employment and income generation and recognised that
forests provide a wide range of goods and services which create opportunities to address
many of the pressing sustainable development challenges. The role of forests and trees in
the provision of goods for rural communities is fundamental to their wellbeing and food
security. Continuum of forest states exists between primary natural forests and plantation
all of which can supply wood, fibre, fuel wood, and non-wood forest products as well as
provide important ecosystem services such as biodiversity conservation, climate
regularisation, carbon storage and water supply. Plantation are able to efficiently produce
high quantities of wood products that may alleviate pressure on natural forests, create job
that support rural development and provide range of ecosystem services, especially when
established on degraded lands.

        Assam, a state characterized by its hills, valleys, and a complex river system
dominated by the mighty Brahmaputra, boasts a diverse range of habitats, from tropical
evergreen rainforests to subtropical forests. According to the National Forest Policy, the
Forest Department is responsible for managing the forests, forest products, and wildlife
within the state's constitutional framework. Covering an area of 78,438 square kilometers,
Assam features four distinct physiographic units: the Brahmaputra Valley, the Barak
Valley, the Karbi-Anglong Plateau, and the North Cachar Hills, all of which are rich in flora
and fauna diversity.




  136
                              Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



       Forestry plays a significant role in Assam's economy. Under the constitutional
provisions, forestry is part of the concurrent list, granting the Forest Department the
authority to manage forests, their products, and oversee wildlife development. The issues
of environmental protection and the conservation of natural resources—particularly flora
and fauna, including medicinal herbs and shrubs—have become increasingly important
from both commercial and conservation perspectives due to their extensive use in natural
products.
       Conservation of forest was given importance since the times of earliest rulers. The
state of Assam is one of the most well-known sites in the world for unique wildlife. The
conservation of various species of endangered wildlife is always a challenging task. Assam
is harbouring the big mammals – like Rhino, Tiger, Gangetic River Dolphin, Asiatic Buffalo
etc. The state of Assam is enriched with extensive forest area and wealth like valuable
forest products and also rich with different species and strains of flora and fauna. People
of Assam from time immemorial have also depended upon the forest to meet their daily
needs. The government of India enacted Schedule Tribes and other forest dwellers
(Recognition of forest rights) Act 2005, for recognition of rights of Schedule Tribes and
other forest dwellers living in forest fringe villages from centuries on their rights to use
forest resources.
       Assam is home to a diverse range of forests, including evergreen, semi-evergreen,
mixed deciduous, moist forests, dry Sal forests, riverine forests, moist savannahs, dry
savannahs, and other miscellaneous forest types. According to the National Forest Policy,
the minimum desired forest cover for proper environmental and ecological security is 33%
in the tropical zone, 60% in the Himalayan and peninsular regions, and 20% in the Great
Plains. Biodiversity estimates for Assam reveal a rich variety of plant and animal species
found within its forests. The following table illustrates the state's significantly rich
biodiversity.

RECORDED FOREST AREA:
   Recorded Forest Area includes all area recorded as forest in Govt. records. Both Forest
cover and Recorded Forest Area (RFA) describe the extent of forest but have different
meanings. The ‘Forest Cover” refers to all tree patches that have canopy density of more
than 10% and area of one hectare or more in size, irrespective of land use, legal status
and ownership. It may include orchards, bamboo, and palms etc. The total recorded forest
area in Assam is 26,836 square km. which is 34.21% of the total geographical area of
Assam and 0.82% of the geographical area of the country. As per PCCF, out of total
recorded forest area, total reserved forest area of the state is 12,808.17 square km. and
Un-classed State Forest constitutes approx.14,028 square km which is 47.72% and
52.28% respectively of the total recorded forest area of the state. It is significant that as
per ISFR 2023 assessment, except Mizoram and Sikkim, other North Eastern states have
lost their Forest cover. The lost area of forest of these states were (1) Arunachal Pradesh
52.49 Sq km, (2) Assam 83.92 Sq. km, (3) Meghalaya 84.07 Sq. km, (4) Manipur 62.20
Sq (5) Tripura 100.70 Sq. km, (6) Nagaland 125.22 Sq. km.At the same time, an increase
in Forest Cover of (7) Mizoram 178.42 Sq. km. and (8) Sikkim 2.88 Sq.km. was seen.
Assam has witnessed a decrease of Dense Forest but an increase of Open Forest and Tree
Cover as per assessment in 2023 by Forest Survey of India, Dehradun over its previous
year ISFR 2021.

Tree Outside Forest in India (TOFI) a new initiative of the Government toward
forest cover:
   Tree Outside forest in India (TOFI) is a new initiative of the Government. State Govt.
also participating in this programme to ward forest cover in Assam outside forest. It is a
five years joint initiative by United State Agency for International Development (USAID)
and Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) of the Govt. of India
with a united force consortium partners led by CIFOR-ICRAF, the initiative committed to
expanding the area under tree outside forest for the benefit of livelihood and ecosystem
in the seven states i.e., Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Haryana, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu&
Uttar Pradesh. This is an effort to support global climate change mitigation and adaption
goals. Assam also hopes that participating with this type of joint ventures will increase
coverage of trees forest area up to 38% and help to create a sustainable eco-friendly zone
& economic environment in the state. Moreover, the Chief Minister of Assam is also very
much concerned about the forest coverage and climatic condition in the state. Launching
of Chief Minister Institutional Plantation Program (CMIPP), 2022 with a same objective
initiated plantation of native plant species named as ‘Amrit Briksha” in the different
institutional premises, coinciding with ‘the Azadi Ka Amrit Mohotsava”.
Amrit Briksha Andolon, 2023-A new initiative toward green economy of Assam.


   In Assam’s efforts to build a green economy, 8 June, 2023 would be marked as a red-
letter day as Hon’ble Chief Minister of Assam announced to launch the “Amrit Briksha
Andolon”, 2023 on that day. To create a revolution among the people in respect of
strengthening the economy through forest/ plantation of commercially viable trees, the
focus has been laid on commercial tree species suitable for timber, plywood making,
medicinal and some more valuable trees like Chandan, Baga Chandan, and fruits which
are abundantly grown in Assam. Amrit Briksha Andolon was successfully carried out on
17th September, 2023 with “Jana bhagidary” model where Self-help Group, ASHA worker,
Anganawadi Worker, Mahila Samitee, Educational Institutions, Tea Garden workers and
Government officials were involved actively to successfully plant more than 1 crore
plantation within 24 hours.

                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26

by a team ( total 921730 nos.) in 24 hours 4)Most trees planted by a team (total 331929

( 47,28,898 nos.)for an environmental sustainability campaign. It is expected that such
type of plantation would help the common people of the state to meet their future need.


3-PRONGED BENEFITS
   The state of Assam will reap three-pronged benefits from the historic Amrit Brikshya
Andolan- Greener Assam, Battling Climate Change and Economic prosperity.


GROWING STOCK IN ASSAM STATE FOREST:
   In simple terms, growing stock is the value of all living trees in the forest area. Periodic
estimation of the growing stock of wood is essential for developing National policies and
strategies for the sustainable use of forest resources. Growing stock is an indicator of the
sustainability and productivity of the forest. Estimation of growing stock inside the forest
and outside the forest is essential for the assessment of the volume of timber or
sustainable use by the people. As per 2023 estimation report, it reveals that the recent
growing stock of Assam both inside and outside the forest, is 120.274 million Cum. and
24.94 million cum (total 145.214 million cum) respectively. Table 10.5 shows the growing
stock of the state. It is revealed from the Table that the ever-increasing stock in the state
has increased in 2023 w.r.t ISFR 2021 assessment.

Wetlands in Reserved Forest and its influence in state economy:
       Wetlands are unique ecosystems that provide water and habitat for a diverse range
of plants and animals. These areas of land are either temporarily or permanently covered


                                                                                        143
                               Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




by water and are a crucial component of the natural resources within our ecosystem.
Currently, there are 7,313 wetlands (excluding rivers and streams) in Assam, covering an
area of 2,43,791 hectares, according to sources from the forest department. This
extensive network of wetlands plays a significant role in Assam's economy, particularly in
supporting the animal husbandry and fishing sectors, which are vital for the rural
livelihoods in the state.
Bio-diversity of forest in Assam:
   Forest biological diversity refers to the diversity within forests at three levels. It
includes all species of plants, animals and microbes occurring in the forest, not just the
tree species. If we take an over view of Assam’s Forest diversity then we witness the
following diversity i.e., Orchid diversity, medicinal plant diversity, Cane diversity, Aquatic
plant diversity, the rich Faunal diversity, Mammalian diversity, Primate diversity, Avian
diversity, Reptilian diversity, Fish diversity, Molluscan diversity and many more. In short,
we may mention that there are 293 nos. orchid, 38 nos. naturally growing bamboo,14
nos. of cane ,952 nos. of medicinal plants,193 nos. species of mammalian, 100 nos.
aquatic species are found in the forest of Assam. Moreover, out of 15 Indian primate
species 9 are found in Assam. Besides these, the Molluscan diversity is one of the most
beautiful creatures on the earth. The IUCN has identified NE Zone as a rich zone of
Swallowtail butterfly under “Swallowtail conservation action Plan”. As per reports by the
IUCN there are 284 species of plants are to be critically endangered, 149 species as
endangered, 58 species as vulnerable and 13 species are nearby threatened. In view of
this, biodiversity of the state needs to be rebuild again. In this respect the state forest
department has identified few thrust areas and initiated the following actions:
        Preservation of the existing bio diversities.
        Arresting the trend of existing degradation and reverting to the process of
         reforestation and extension of the forestry with multiple stake holders.
        Preservation and development of the existing protected area network and their
         expansion in suitable areas.
        Development activities and research in forestry and wildlife.
        Bridging the gaps in infrastructural and logistical fronts.


BAMBOO RESOURCES IN THE FOREST OF ASSAM:
   Bamboo the most versatile group of plants in the grass family belongs to the sub-
family bambusoideae of the family of Poaceae (Gramineae). Bamboos are one of the
fastest growing perennial plants in the world. The North East region of India has the
highest concentration of bamboo, accounting for more than 60% of the total bamboo
resources of the country as a whole. Assam is rich in bamboo resources and most of its
forest is richly stocked with bamboo and cane of various species. Assam bearing only 7.27
% of total country’s bearing area. There are no exclusive bamboo forests in the plains of
Assam. Pure bamboo forest occurred in N.C. Hills and Karbi-Anglong district. Total bamboo
bearing tree area in the country is 1,54,670 Sq. km. as per 2023 ISFR report, compared
to 1,49,443 Sq. km. in 2021 as per ISFR, increase of 5227 Sq. km. However, the bamboo
bearing area in Assam increased to 11,246 Sq. km. in 2023 against 10,659 Sq. km. in
2021. Due to versatile character of bamboo it’s capable of providing ecological, economic
and livelihood security to the people. It is an integral part of the lifestyle and economy of



   144
                            Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



Assam. There are 38 numbers of Bamboo species found in the Assam Forest area as
reported by the forest department. For promotion of bamboo sector in the government of
India and government of Assam taken many initiatives to further develop its potentiality.
Assam has become the first country’s state of the art Bamboo Technology Park to boost
cultivation in the state and the region. Recently to boost the Rural economy of Assam,
Govt. has initiated to establish Bamboo Industrial Park in the state with collaboration of
the DoNER Ministry G.O.I. which will help the local entrepreneur to establish MSME for
their sustainable development. Bamboo contributes to subsistence need of about 2.5
billion people around the world. Mamboosa Jaintiana and Melocanna arundiana are the
species reported only from Assam. Bamboos are cultivated in every household of Assam
and people of rural area typically depend on bamboo to meet their recurring micro needs.
The following Table-10.5 shows the growing stock of bamboo inside the recorded forest
areas which includes culms of one year of age. It is very clear that Assam is in a significant
position in respect of area of bearing trees and production also.
FOREST ROADS:

   The state forest department is entrusted the task of maintenance and management of
forest, forest product and wildlife in the state. For the purpose of patrolling inside the
forest   area of Assam, to harvest the forest produces, and for both improvement,
development and creation of infrastructure, the existence of proper roads in the forests
are very essential. The forest department of Assam has given special        emphasis on this
matter and proposed to improve the road connectivity for better protection and
conservation of forest biodiversity and wildlife. Till 2025, there are 1825 km. surfaced,
24779 km. unsurfaced, 12513 km. motorable and 10947 km. non-motorable forest road
in Assam.
OUT TURN OF FOREST PRODUCE & REVENUE:

    Forests are sources of natural resources to be used for various manufacturing
activities. In the context of conservation, forests are however not seen as a revenue
generation source. The forests are, however, a source of livelihood of people living in forest
fringe villages. The forests produced in the state are being harvested following the laid
the principles of working plan of forest to ensure sustainability. Major forest produce in
the state include industrial wood namely Teak, Shisam, Sal, Chir, Kait, Hollong, Makai,
etc. and other products like pulp, match wood, round wood and fuel wood; minor forest
products including bamboo, Broom Grass, Biri Leaves etc. At present, however, the major
source of forest revenue are sand, gravel, stone, silt, clay, thatch etc. This out turn of
forest have been contributing to Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP), so it is very
essential to estimate their growing value. During 2023-24 the total out turn of Forest
Department is Rs.4581.469 crore and during 2024-25 the total out turn is 5337.882 crore.
The out turns of various forest produce in the state are presented in Table 10.6 and
revenue generated from forests sources in the state are shown in Table 10.7. The Assam
Govt. has now given importance to increasing the plantation area of Agarwood and
Medicinal plants, and commercial wood in the state, expecting high-valued Agar oil
medicinal plants to boost the income especially at the microeconomic level to contribute
to the state economy

FOREST AND INDUSTRY:
   Forests not only provide invaluable ecological services to the nation, but they also
contribute significantly to environmental security. Additionally, forests play a crucial role
in the economy, especially for rural and marginalized communities. They are rich sources
of timber, small timber, firewood, and bamboo. Furthermore, forests create opportunities
for establishing forest-based industries, such as sawmills and plywood and veneer
manufacturing units, as well as small-scale industries like building materials, furniture
businesses, and cane and SitalPati enterprises. These industries employ large numbers of
youth, both directly and indirectly.
   The government has emphasized the importance of planting Agar and Chandan
saplings to encourage economic development among the general population in the state.
Moreover, forest tourism, including various national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, offers
employment opportunities for unemployed youth as safari guides for local and foreign
tourists.
         In summary, the forest sector plays a vital role in the state’s economy. However,
despite the sector's significant potential, the government should take more initiatives to
support and uplift it.

PROTECTED AREA - NATIONAL PARK AND WILDLIFE SANCTUARIES
   The Protected Area Network (PAN) of Assam includes 8 National parks and 17 wildlife
sanctuaries covering an area of about 5459.38 sq.km. constituting approximate 6.96
percent of the total geographical area of the state. Presently there are four Tiger reserves
in Assam. The wildlife sanctuaries in Assam are a heterogeneous mixture of a variety of
landscapes, plants, birds and animals. Suitable climatic conditions, geographical location
and vast forest reserves have made Assam a favourable habitat for birds, animals and
natural vegetation. The wildlife sanctuaries and national parks of the state are the breeding
ground for some of the rarest global species. Many wildlife sanctuaries of Assam are home
to large number of precious wildlife species from the golden langur to the one horned
rhinoceros. Two national parks of the state are designated as world heritage sites by the
UNESCO in 1985.

 CONSERVATION OF WILDLIFE: THE EIGHT NATIONAL PARKS OF ASSAM:
    At present there are eight national parks in the state and out of these two national
 parks Kaziranga and Manas of the state are recognised by UNESCO as world heritage sites.
 The brief notes on these National Parks are as below:
1. Kaziranga National Park:
    The Kaziranga National Park spread across the floodplains of the Brahmaputra River.
 Its forests, wetlands and grasslands are home to deer, tiger, elephant and one horned
 Rhinoceros .It also has the world’s largest population of Asiatic Wild Buffalos and nearly
 500 species of birds. It is known by world as one of the one horned Rhinoceroses home.
 Not just this, it’s a vibrant and beautiful Tiger Reserve that hold some special and
 significant position in the wild life map of India. In every year, large number of tourist
 from home country and abroad visited to this National Park and enjoy their natural beauty.
 During 2024-25, total 388871 Nos. of Domestic and 17693 Nos. Foreign tourist visited to
 Kaziranga National Park


 2. Manas National Park:
    Manas National Park was declared as World heritage site by UNESCO in 1985.MNP is
 also declared as project tiger reserve, elephant reserve and a biosphere reserve. The Park
 is located in the Himalayan foothills and is contiguous with the Royal Manas National Park
 in Bhutan, covering an area of about 850 sq km. The Park is known for its rare and
 endangered endemic wild life such as the Assam roofed turtle, hispid hare, golden langur
 and pygmy hog. During 2024-25, total 59468 Nos. Domestic and 3367 Nos. Foreign tourist
 visited to Manas National Park.


 3. Orang National Park:
    The Orang National Park is located on the north bank of the river Brahmaputra in the
 Darrang and Sonitpur districts of Assam. It covers an area of 279.28sq km. The landscape,
 flora and fauna of Orang National Park are similar to those of Kaziranga National Park. It
 was established as a sanctuary in 1985 and declared a National Park on 8th April, 1999.
 The park has a rich of flora fauna, including the great Indian one horned rhinoceros, pygmy
 hog, elephants, wild buffalos, and tiger. During 2024-25, total 2787 Nos. Domestic and
 56 Nos. Foreign tourist visited to Orang National Park.
 4. Nameri National Park:
    Declared as a National Park in 1978, Nameri National Park is in the foot hills of the
 eastern Himalayas in the Sonitpur district of Assam, and about 35 km from Tezpur town.
 The Park covers an area of 200 sq km. The Park is the second tiger reserve of Assam and
 is also important for the commutation of elephants. Apart from 30 species of mammals
 recorded in this area, the rich wildlife includes tiger, black bear, elephant, leopard, clouded
 leopard, pangoline, Indian wild dog, deer, calved cat, capped langur, jackals etc. various
 species of birds such as endangered white winged wood duck, four species of hornbill,
 butterflies and reptiles are also found in the park, A large numbers of tourist visited to this
 park in every year. During 2024-25, total 9414 Nos. Domestic and 1373 Nos. Foreign
 tourist visited to Nameri National Park.




   152
                              Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26



5. Dibru-Saikhowa National Park:
   Dibru-Saikhowa National Park is situated in the Dibrugarh and Tinsukia districts of
Assam, India. Established as a Biosphere Reserve in 1995, it covers an area of 340 square
kilometers. The park primarily consists of moist semi-evergreen forests, canebrakes, and
grasslands. It is the longest swamp forest in Northeast India, characterized by a tropical
monsoon climate that features hot and humid summers, followed by cool and typically dry
winters.
   This national park is a haven for many endangered species and boasts rich fish
diversity. Visitors can observe various animal species in their natural habitats, including
the Royal Bengal Tiger, Hoolock Gibbons, and Leopards. Additionally, it supports a number
of bird species with restricted ranges.
   During the 2024-25 period, a total of 2,939 domestic tourists and 24 foreign tourists
visited Dibru-Saikhowa National Park.
6. Raimona National Park:
     In the month of June 2021 Government of Assam declared the State’s Six National
Park Called Raimona National Park named after the historical Capital of Bijni estate
Raimona. It is spreading over 422 sq.km. in the Kokrajhar District under Bodoland
Territorial Region (BTR) combining part of RipuChirang Reserve Forest. Raimona is a
home of legendary elephant and rare butterfly and also Gee’s Golden Langur, the one of
the most endangered Primates of the world. During 2024-25, total 3575 Nos. Domestic
and 06 Nos. Foreign tourist visited to Raimona National Park.


7. Dihing Patkai National Park:
   Dihing Patkai National Park as 7th National Park of the state declared by Govt of Assam
in the month of June, 2021. After declaration of this park, Assam now becomes the second
state having highest National Parks in country. The area of this park is around 234.26 sq.
km. located in the district of Dibrugrah and Tinsukia. It is believed to be the last remaining
contiguous for major elephant habitat and 310 species of butterflies and tiger and clouded
leopard. During 2024-25, total 1239 Nos. Domestic and 12 Nos. Foreign tourist visited to
DihingPatkai National Park.


8. SikhnaJahwlao National Park:
   SikhnaJahwlao National Park as 8th National Park of the state declared by Govt of
Assam in the month of March, 2025. It is spreading over 316.29 Sq.km in the Kokrajhar
and Chirang District.


BIOSPHERE RESERVES
   Biosphere Reserves are areas of natural and cultural landscapes extending over large
areas of terrestrial or coastal/marine ecosystems. Biosphere Reserve (BR) is an
international designation given by UNESCO. The biosphere reserve network was launched
in 1971 by UNESCO, after the initiation of MAB-Man and Biosphere Program.

NATIONAL RHINO VISION:
   Indian Rhino Vision (IRV) 2020 is a joint program of Assam Forest Department.It is a
multi-partner program where Govt. has joined hands with the international agencies and
local communities.
Rhino protection in Assam:
   At present protection of the world famous one horned Rhinocerous in Assam is one of
the challenging tasks of the Government. Kaziranga is the home land of this world famous
one horned Rhino where its successful conservation can be illustrated with more than 85%
of Rhino present in Kaziranga National Park. After formation of the present Government,
it has adopted zero tolerance in respect of poaching and wild life crime. To conserve the
Rhino, Govt. has initiated some strong steps like constituting of Fast Track Courts,
Formation of Anti Rhino Poaching Task Force, Deployment of Additional Forces, Used
Unmanned Areal Aircraft (Drone), Modernisation of Arms and Ammunitions and creation
of Special Rhino Protection Force with 112 nos. of personnel etc. Due to these strong steps
of the Govt. the poaching of one horned Rhino in the state has decreased significantly.
Data reveals that during 2013 & 2014, the Rhino poaching was 27, but from 2015 it was
decreased to 17, 2016 it was 18, 2017 it was 6, 2018 it was 7, in 2019 it was 3, in 2020
it was 2 and in 2021 it    was only 1.Govt. has expected that if the protection mechanism
will do their work perfectly the rhino poaching in near future could be controlled which is
also a big dream of the state Govt. as well as the people of the state.

   Assam State Zoo and Botanical Garden was established in the year 1957 with an area
of 175 hect in the heart of Guwahati metro city. Presently, Assam State exhibits an
impressive collection of 526 mammals, 576 birds, and 78 reptiles belonging to 112 species,
both indigenous and exotic. From the revenue point of view, this zoo has a great potential
in future. The following table shows the trend of visitors and revenue collection of this Zoo

PROJECTS ON CONSERVATION OF FORESTS AND WILDLIFE:

Centre for Wildlife Rehabilitation and Conservation:
   It is known to all that in every year like human illness, animals also suffering from
different morbidities and faces endangered situation. To rehabilitate and conserve this
wildlife, in August, 2002 Government has established Centre for Wildlife Rehabilitation and
Conservation (CWRC) through an MoU between Assam Forest Department and Wildlife
Trust of India to provide emergency care, treatment, and rehabilitation of indigenous wild
animals that are displaced due to various reasons-clouded leopards, black leopards, black
bears, wild buffalos and many other important taxa in India. CWRC is situated near


                                                                                                 155
                             Economic Survey, Assam, 2025-26




Kaziranga National Park. Four Mobile Veterinary Service (MVS) facilities are also attached
to CWRC, Kaziranga and situated in Dhola, Diphu, Kokrajhar and Seijusa. So far, CWRC
has handled 4545 number of rescued animals of 246 different species.
The Pigmy Hog Conservation Program (PHCP):
        Pigmy hog (Porculasaluania) (local Assamese name is NalGahari) is the smallest
species of wild pig extremely rare in the wild. It is found only in Manas National Park in
Assam. An adult male weighs 8 to 9 kg and their life span is only 8-10 years. For
conservation of this endangered species, the Assam Forest department in collaboration
with Durrel Wildlife Conservation Trust, IUCN/SSC Wild pig Specialist Group, Ministry of
Environment & forest -Govt. of India, Eco-systems-India started the Pygmy Hog
Conservation Programme (PHCP) with breeding of pygmy Hog in the year 1996.PHCP
maintains a captive population of about 70 hogs and has reintroduced 108 hogs over ten
years in SonaiRupai Wildlife Sanctuary, RG Orang National Park and Barnadi Wildlife
Sanctuary in Assam.
Project Tiger:
        Assam has four tiger reserves namely Orang, Kaziranga, Manas and Nameri. The
first country wide tiger census was conducted in 1972 and estimated about 1800 tiger
population. The tiger conservation programme, Project Tiger was launched in 1st April
1973 by the government of India. The project aims at ensuring a viable population of
Bengal tigers in their natural habitats, protecting them from extinction and preserving area
of biological importance as a natural heritage. The Government has taken up necessary
action for intensive protection of tiger areas and stopping poaching. During 2020-21,
Government has spent Rs. 460.042 lakh for Manas National Park, Rs. 131.89 lakh for
Nameri National Park and Rs. 307.098 lakh for Orang National Park for all round
development.
